slides: Open by making projective geometry the geometry of incidence after parallelism has been absorbed into points at infinity. The chapter repeatedly asks what survives projective motion: joins, meets, collinearity, cross-ratio, conic polarity, Pascal lines, reguli, and the absolute structure used to recover Euclidean geometry.

Use the route slide to keep the chapter navigable. We move from projective-plane axioms to homogeneous coordinates, then to Desargues, harmonic ranges, projectivities, homographies, conic polarity, Pascal's theorem, ruled quadrics in space, and finally Euclidean orthogonality as extra projective data.

The projective-plane axiom slide should make the line at infinity feel like an incidence repair rather than an exotic add-on. In the finite model, every pair of points has a unique join and every pair of lines has a unique meet, so parallel exceptional cases disappear.

Homogeneous coordinates are the computational language of the chapter. Points and lines are dual three-vectors, joins and meets are cross products, and incidence is a dot product equal to zero. The displayed example verifies both join and meet incidences exactly.

Desargues is the first major incidence theorem in the deck. Three connector lines pass through one center, and the corresponding side intersections fall on one axis. The residuals are at numerical roundoff, so the diagram is an inspected projective configuration rather than a sketch.

Harmonic sets and projectivities introduce the cross-ratio as the projective measurement that survives. The complete quadrangle produces a cross-ratio of negative one, and the interactive projectivity preserves a nontrivial cross-ratio even though the point parameters move.

The homography lab is the practical collineation test. A projective warp fits the four corner correspondences exactly and keeps a row nearly collinear, while the cross-ratio on that row is preserved. The adjacent length ratio changes, which is the warning against metric intuition.

Conics organize projective duality. A symmetric bilinear form sends a point to its polar line, tangent incidence is checked at a conic point, and Pascal's theorem sends three opposite-side intersections from six conic points onto a single Pascal line.

The projective-space slide lifts the same vocabulary into three dimensions. A ruled quadric contains two families of generators with tiny residuals, and the Euclidean absolute-polarity lab shows that orthogonality is recovered only after adding the absolute at infinity.

Close by emphasizing the hierarchy. Projective geometry preserves incidence and cross-ratio; affine geometry returns when a line at infinity is chosen; Euclidean geometry returns when an absolute polarity is chosen. The chapter's artifacts demonstrate each added structure as a checked invariant.
